{"id": "28:77/q27", "question": "What broader counsel on worldly life is transmitted with the verse?", "turns_on": "The sayings emphasize either life's brevity or balance with lawful worldly needs.", "positions": [{"id": "28:77/q27/p1", "position": "Use temporary life for the afterlife and avoid destructive attachment to abundance.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports that afterlife focus brings inner sufficiency while world focus brings poverty and disorder; life is a test and little remains. ʿAlī calls life preparation for a contest, warns of desires and long hopes, and values good deeds above gains. Ibn Qutayba explains spring growth as warning of excess. Al-Sulamī makes the world serve the afterlife and God; al-Biqāʿī adds ascetic nearness; al-Bursawī's couplet says treasure remains only when given away."}, {"id": "28:77/q27/p2", "position": "Cultivate lawful worldly welfare while pursuing the afterlife.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿUmar says work for this world as if living forever and for the next as if dying tomorrow; Study Quran records alternative attribution to Prophet or ʿAlī. Al-Jishumī's Judge says seek covers duties and do not forget covers the self's rightful desires. Saʿdī says eat and give generously to win both."}]}
{"id": "28:77/q28", "question": "Which report urges seizing opportunities before they pass?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:77/q28/p1", "position": "The Prophet urged taking youth, health, wealth, free time and life before their opposites.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī reports it through ʿAmr ibn Maymūn and calls it mursal; al-Bursawī repeats it. Al-Rāzī reports a related exhortation to prepare before old age and death, after which Paradise or Hell remains."}]}
{"id": "28:77/q29", "question": "What other sayings accompany the verse's discussion?", "turns_on": "These are distinct ancillary sayings.", "positions": [{"id": "28:77/q29/p1", "position": "Transmit religious knowledge, since its receiver may understand better.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports the prophetic exhortation."}, {"id": "28:77/q29/p2", "position": "Sincerity, counsel to leaders and community adherence preserve hearts.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports this saying of the Prophet."}, {"id": "28:77/q29/p3", "position": "Fear of others must not stop speaking known truth.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī reports the Prophet's warning."}, {"id": "28:77/q29/p4", "position": "Reformers replace vices with virtues and gain God's love.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī's Najmī source describes the abdal replacing ignorance with knowledge, miserliness with generosity, greed with chastity, injustice with justice, rashness with deliberation, and corruption with righteousness."}]}
{"id": "28:77/q30", "question": "What ancillary lexical and proverbial explanations appear with these notes?", "turns_on": "These are separate ancillary lexical observations.", "positions": [{"id": "28:77/q30/p1", "position": "The hundred camels saying distinguishes a herd from the rare conspicuous riding camel.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba calls the pasture herd hunayda, identifies the riding camel by maturity and appearance, and takes the comparison to teach equal law and retaliation regardless of rank, like the comb-teeth and donkey-teeth sayings."}, {"id": "28:77/q30/p2", "position": "Ḥabaṭ is a camel's belly swelling from overgrazing; yulam means nearly killing it.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba explains these terms in the warning about destructive spring growth."}, {"id": "28:77/q30/p3", "position": "Settling like a gazelle means staying quietly inactive in a house.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba compares this with a gazelle in its lair."}, {"id": "28:77/q30/p4", "position": "Clothed yet naked describes thin garments that do not cover.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba applies it to women."}, {"id": "28:77/q30/p5", "position": "A closed bag in a peace document signifies a loyal heart free of rancor.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba calls chests ʿiyāb and cites an unnamed poet."}, {"id": "28:77/q30/p6", "position": "Few is a relative quantity without a fixed measure.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī contrasts it with many; he also says usury's growth tends to loss, records a proverb for unknown lineage, describes qilla as an unspecified lifted amount with a drinking poem and as a mountain peak, and says istaqalla means departing."}, {"id": "28:77/q30/p7", "position": "Lā can negate and can convey lam.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites a poem and separately notes prohibition in this verse."}, {"id": "28:77/q30/p8", "position": "The root ḥ-s-n also conveys beauty and virtue.", "reasons": "Study Quran notes the root's semantic range."}]}
{"id": "28:77/q31", "question": "What ancillary classification and reciter notices are supplied?", "turns_on": "The notices concern separate facts.", "positions": [{"id": "28:77/q31/p1", "position": "The entire Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ is Meccan.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī attributes this to al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ and ʿIkrima."}, {"id": "28:77/q31/p2", "position": "Ibn al-Naffākh was a trustworthy Egyptian hadith scholar of simple life who died in 314 AH.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī reports Ibn Yūnus's notice."}, {"id": "28:77/q31/p3", "position": "Ibn Nahshal was a precise and virtuous recitation imam at Isfahan's mosque who died in 294 AH.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī records his office and reputation."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q01", "question": "How does Qarun's reply answer his advisers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q01/p1", "position": "He silences their advice by crediting himself and denying an unearned favor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says he evades their demand; al-Rāzī calls the prior counsel complete. Al-Biqāʿī says إنما restricts the cause and the passive obscures the giver. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the particle and its spelling; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says he omits God and claims freedom to pursue luxury and power. Ibn ʿAbbās says Qarun's self-crediting rejected God's gift; ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith contrasts Solomon's acknowledgment of grace at 27:40."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q02", "question": "What is the thing Qarun says he was given?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q02/p1", "position": "His wealth or treasures.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr traces it to 'what God gave you' in 28:77; the passive leaves the giver implicit."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q03", "question": "What does Qarun mean by claiming he received it on knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether ʿilm is Qarun's virtue, scripture, skill or specialized art, or God's knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q03/p1", "position": "His merit or superior learning entitled him to wealth and proved divine favor.", "reasons": "Qatāda, Muqātil, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddī report this; Ibn Kathīr compares 39:49 and 41:50, al-Ṭabrisī 18:36."}, {"id": "28:78/q03/p2", "position": "He credited practical skill in trade, farming and earning.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā ibn Sallām and Ibn ʿĪsā give acquisition skill; Abū Sulaymān gives effort. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ cites 39:52 and 40:82–83."}, {"id": "28:78/q03/p3", "position": "He meant alchemy or gold-making.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Kalbī are cited. Al-Zajjāj, Ibn Kathīr and Abū Ḥayyān object; the transmission accounts differ."}, {"id": "28:78/q03/p4", "position": "He meant Torah learning, in which he excelled.", "reasons": "Abū Isḥāq and others identify Torah knowledge; some call him Israel's leading reader, and al-Qurṭubī one of Moses's seventy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it deceitful display."}, {"id": "28:78/q03/p5", "position": "He believed God knowingly selected him or knew good in him; ʿindī conveys his judgment.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd and Abū Zayd take ʿilm as divine knowledge. Al-Ālūsī also gives ʿilm as 'the known thing,' citing 2:255. Study Quran notes that ʿalā ʿilm elsewhere can denote divine knowledge, citing 7:52, 39:49, 44:32 and 45:23, while leaving the exact sense open."}, {"id": "28:78/q03/p6", "position": "He knew how to extract buried treasures.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says this proposal presupposes a real extraction craft; he leaves its truth uncertain."}, {"id": "28:78/q03/p7", "position": "He invoked God by the Greatest Name for wealth.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports this but prefers the merit explanation."}, {"id": "28:78/q03/p8", "position": "He knew Joseph's treasures.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī lists it."}, {"id": "28:78/q03/p9", "position": "He was a goldsmith.", "reasons": "Study Quran says commentators report and dismiss this."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q04", "question": "How is 'on knowledge' construed?", "turns_on": "Attachment and the agent of knowledge differ.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q04/p1", "position": "It is circumstantial to the passive verb's subject.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says most grammarians use it to express Qarun's claimed entitlement."}, {"id": "28:78/q04/p2", "position": "It attaches causally to 'I was given.'", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says ʿalā can express superiority or cause."}, {"id": "28:78/q04/p3", "position": "The verbal noun 'knowledge' can be Qarun's or God's.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān gives both; Ibn ʿĀshūr mentions further undetailed analyses."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q05", "question": "How did Qarun allegedly acquire alchemy?", "turns_on": "The teachers and route of transmission vary.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q05/p1", "position": "Moses divided the art among Qarun, Joshua and Caleb; Qarun tricked the others into sharing.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and al-Ḍaḥḥāk are cited; al-Rāzī specifies lead to silver and copper to gold."}, {"id": "28:78/q05/p2", "position": "Moses taught his sister, who taught Qarun.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī calls her Qarun's wife; Bursawī names her Kulthūm."}, {"id": "28:78/q05/p3", "position": "Moses, Joshua and Aaron or his sons supplied separate shares.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqāsh's versions vary on teachers, shares and deception."}, {"id": "28:78/q05/p4", "position": "The attribution is doubtful.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān doubts it and cites al-Zajjāj; al-Ālūsī says a miracle could not have belonged to Qaru

{"id": "28:78/q06", "question": "What story explains Qarun's move from worship to wealth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q06/p1", "position": "Iblis gradually redirected forty years of worship into work and attachment to wealth.", "reasons": "Abū Sulaymān al-Dārānī says Iblis outdid Qarun in worship, persuaded him to abandon communal and charitable duties, then alternate work with worship, after which wealth poured in. Bursawī retells the progression."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q07", "question": "Is alchemy a real and possible craft?", "turns_on": "Whether metals share a species, whether craft prepares a God-created form, and whether a reliable method exists.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q07/p1", "position": "Human craft cannot genuinely transmute metal.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj calls alchemy unreal. Ibn Kathīr says only God changes created kinds, citing 22:73 and a hadith challenge. Ibn Sīnā treats metals as distinct species. Other objections cite unknown ratios, fire resistance, art versus nature, mines, gold's economic rarity, absence of a reproducible method and a faulty yeast analogy."}, {"id": "28:78/q07/p2", "position": "It is a possible but very difficult natural craft.", "reasons": "Bursawī cites purification, saints and personal witness. Al-Fārābī and Ibn Bājjah treat metals as one species with alterable qualities. Al-Tughrāʾī says craft prepares matter for a God-created form; al-Rāzī argues from medicine, antidotes, heat, artificial fire and salts. Al-Ālūsī favors a rare hidden craft and answers Ibn Khaldūn's objections."}, {"id": "28:78/q07/p3", "position": "A real transmutation would be a miracle, wonder or other supernatural effect.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites Ḥaywa ibn Shurayḥ's God-given wonder; Ibn Khaldūn likens it to walking on water. Al-Ṭībī suggests a miracle, which al-Ālūsī says cannot fit Qarun."}, {"id": "28:78/q07/p4", "position": "Its ontological or practical possibility remains unresolved.", "reasons": "Ibn Sīnā admits coloring metals but doubts a changed species form; al-Rāzī says visible differences may be accidental. Al-Ālūsī notes scholarly vacillation."}, {"id": "28:78/q07/p5", "position": "Practitioners propose accelerated natural mineral growth or an elixir.", "reasons": "Ibn Khaldūn describes intensified natural powers over 1,080 great solar cycles, or a yeast-like elixir; this would require knowledge of element ratios, innate heat and every stage."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q08", "question": "What does the word 'alchemy' itself derive from?", "turns_on": "The proposed source language and derivation differ.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q08/p1", "position": "It may be Greek, meaning artifice or trick.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this etymology."}, {"id": "28:78/q08/p2", "position": "It may derive from Hebrew words meaning 'it is from God.'", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this proposed derivation."}, {"id": "28:78/q08/p3", "position": "It may derive from Persian words meaning 'when by a particular method.'", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this proposed derivation."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q09", "question": "What accounts explain alchemy's origin and concealment?", "turns_on": "The alleged transmission and reliability of the accounts differ.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q09/p1", "position": "The art came by revelation and passed among prophets and sages.", "reasons": "Ars, Hermes, Marya, Dhu Simus, al-Ṭughrāʾī and al-Ṭarsūsī link it variously to Seth, Moses, Joseph, Solomon and Adam. An ungraded report mentions the Prophet and white and red sulfur; reports also name Jaʿfar and ʿAlī. Al-Ālūsī doubts hadith authenticity."}, {"id": "28:78/q09/p2", "position": "Sages hid it in symbols and taught selected readers.", "reasons": "Jābir says secrecy protects work and the economy; al-Ālūsī says literal readers are misled and qualified teachers rare."}, {"id": "28:78/q09/p3", "position": "Modern claimants include swindlers and ignorant seekers.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites greed, false hopes and neglected work; al-Ṭughrāʾī faults Ibn Sīnā's missing mixtures, weights, stages and tools."}, {"id": "28:78/q09/p4", "position": "Claims of prophetic authority remain unverified.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says accepted hadith would be widespread and notes Ibn Taymiyya's rejection and a qualified claim about Najm al-Dīn al-Baghdādī."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q10", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from Qarun?", "turns_on": "Self-crediting versus recognition of divine grace.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q10/p1", "position": "Self-admiration and claims to one's own states or deeds bring ruin; the fortunate see God's favor.", "reasons": "Sahl links outward sinking to inward loss of protection, ingratitude and inflated power. Al-Qushayrī calls imagined independent agency deadly poison; Bursawī cites Hafez and Saib on pride."}, {"id": "28:78/q10/p2", "position": "Knowledge should first be attributed to God.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says God creates necessary knowledge and makes acquired knowledge possible."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q11", "question": "What does 'with me' mean and how does it attach?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase locates knowledge or qualifies the claim as Qarun's judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q11/p1", "position": "It means 'in my opinion' and attaches to the gift or stands as an independent clause.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zamakhsharī compare 39:49; al-Kashf prefers an omitted-subject sentence."}, {"id": "28:78/q11/p2", "position": "It modifies 'knowledge': knowledge in Qarun's possession.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī permit it; Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers this as fitting the rebuke."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q12", "question": "How is the final yāʾ of 'with me' read?", "turns_on": "Transmission determines opening or stilling the yāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q12/p1", "position": "Nāfiʿ, Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAmr open it; Ibn Kathīr varies by route.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid lists related yāʾs; Ibn al-Jazarī differentiates Maghribi, Egyptian and Iraqi routes. Qiraat-ER says the dialectal difference has no semantic effect."}, {"id": "28:78/q12/p2", "position": "Other readers leave it quiescent.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī gives the opposing reading."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q13", "question": "What does 'Did he not know?' imply?", "turns_on": "Known history ignored versus genuinely absent useful knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q13/p1", "position": "Qarun knew or could know earlier fates but ignored them.", "reasons": "The Torah, Moses and historians could teach him. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads astonished rebuke; al-Iṣlāḥī cites Pharaoh's drowning; Bursawī quotes a Persian warning against trusting wealth."}, {"id": "28:78/q13/p2", "position": "The question denies he had useful knowledge despite his boast.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī contrasts claimed merit with ignorance of historical lessons; al-Ālūsī supplies elliptical and circumstantial parsings."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q14", "question": "Who are the earlier destroyed generations?", "turns_on": "Different named examples are supplied for the collective.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q14/p1", "position": "Earlier unbelievers who denied messengers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī names ʿĀd, Thamūd and Lot's people."}, {"id": "28:78/q14/p2", "position": "Nimrod ibn Canaan is one named example.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil name him; Bursawī notes his riches."}, {"id": "28:78/q14/p3", "position": "Pharaoh is one named example.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says he consulted Qarun yet perished; al-Iṣlāḥī cites his drowning."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q15", "question": "Why include 'before him'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q15/p1", "position": "It restricts comparison to preceding generations.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says omission of min would widen the scope."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q16", "question": "What does 'generations' mean?", "turns_on": "Temporal definition and etymological image.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q16/p1", "position": "A people living in one period.", "reasons": "Bursawī gives this gloss."}, {"id": "28:78/q16/p2", "position": "The word evokes the hardness of horns.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī gives this etymological image."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q17", "question": "How are the phrases about the past generations parsed?", "turns_on": "Attachment of the phrases.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q17/p1", "position": "'Who' is the object of 'destroyed,' relative or qualified indefinite.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives both analyses."}, {"id": "28:78/q17/p2", "position": "'Before him' attaches to 'destroyed.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives this attachment."}, {"id": "28:78/q17/p3", "position": "'From the generations' attaches to 'destroyed' or qualifies 'who is stronger.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives both."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q18", "question": "What is the greater 'strength'?", "turns_on": "The scope of power.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q18/p1", "position": "Bodily, military or material power.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī gives equipment; Bursawī numbers; al-Iṣlāḥī weapons and grandeur; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 8:60."}, {"id": "28:78/q18/p2", "position": "Moral, intellectual or devotional strength.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī adds knowledge; al-Ālūsī moral power; Bursawī worship, comparing Iblis."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q19", "question": "What is a 'greater gathering'?", "turns_on": "Collected property, people or, in one report, knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q19/p1", "position": "More followers, servants, helpers, family or tribe.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives a gathered group and transmits a count of 250 Israelite leaders among Qarun's followers; al-Iṣlāḥī specifies family or tribe."}, {"id": "28:78/q19/p2", "position": "More accumulated property.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others allow amassed wealth."}, {"id": "28:78/q19/p3", "position": "More knowledge and worship.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports this with Iblis as comparison."}]}

Ibn Kathīr names unbelief and ingratitude. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ says earlier peoples too had prosperity through skill; Study Quran cites 6:6, 19:74, 40:82, 47:13, 50:36."}, {"id": "28:78/q20/p2", "position": "They were destroyed for denying messengers or wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī specify denial; others call them unbelievers."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q21", "question": "Whose sins does 'their sins' mean?", "turns_on": "The antecedent may be the criminals or the destroyed peoples.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q21/p1", "position": "The earlier generations' sins, about which later criminals are not asked.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb give this antecedent; al-Wāḥidī calls it weak and al-Ālūsī dismisses it."}, {"id": "28:78/q21/p2", "position": "The criminals' own sins.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers this: no innocent person is asked for another's sin. Al-Ālūsī also uses this antecedent."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q22", "question": "In what sense are criminals not asked about sins?", "turns_on": "Whether denial concerns accounting, information, identification, excuse, or immediate worldly punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q22/p1", "position": "Angels recognize criminals by their marks.", "reasons": "Mujāhid cites 55:41: blue eyes and blackened faces; al-Ṭabrisī adds seizure by forelocks and feet. Al-Wāḥidī objects that the verse concerns sins, not identification."}, {"id": "28:78/q22/p2", "position": "They enter punishment without reckoning or questioning.", "reasons": "Qatāda and al-Suddī say punishment is direct; al-Qurṭubī says sins are too many and obvious. Al-Wāḥidī prefers Qatāda. Kuranyolu disputes an inference that accountability vanishes."}, {"id": "28:78/q22/p3", "position": "God needs no inquiry because He already knows the facts.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī contrasts human rulers who lack knowledge; records, limbs and manifest guilt furnish further evidence. Kuranyolu retains accountability."}, {"id": "28:78/q22/p4", "position": "The denied question seeks information; questioning elsewhere is rebuke.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others distinguish inquiry from reproach, citing 15:92, 37:24 and 55:39."}, {"id": "28:78/q22/p5", "position": "They cannot present excuses, amends or a plea for satisfaction.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr cites 30:57; Abū Muslim prefers denial of amends, citing 16:84 and 77:35–36. Al-Qurṭubī cites 41:24."}, {"id": "28:78/q22/p6", "position": "Later wrongdoers are not asked about earlier nations' sins or fates.", "reasons": "Muqātil says God recorded those deeds; Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb says later people failed to learn from them. Al-Wāḥidī calls Muqātil's reading weak."}, {"id": "28:78/q22/p7", "position": "In this world God can seize them suddenly without further hearing.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the messengers' prior clarification, 6:44 and an ungraded prophetic report; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ prefers this context."}, {"id": "28:78/q22/p8", "position": "They receive records and confess without enumerating sins orally.", "reasons": "Al-Rabīʿ says they cannot allege injustice, though they may object to accounting."}, {"id": "28:78/q22/p9", "position": "The warning states manifest guilt and certain ruin while retaining accountability.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu rejects the idea that no accounting occurs; al-Biqāʿī says the noun 'criminals' makes the cause explicit and derives جرم from wrongful severing and joining."}]}
{"id": "28:78/q23", "question": "Does the final sentence concern this world or Judgment?", "turns_on": "Immediate worldly context versus Judgment scene.", "positions": [{"id": "28:78/q23/p1", "position": "It concerns worldly destruction or seizure.", "reasons": "Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb joins it to earlier destruction; Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ read sudden worldly punishment. Al-Ālūsī rejects this."}, {"id": "28:78/q23/p2", "position": "It is an afterlife warning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a Resurrection scene; al-Ālūsī prefers an extension to the harsher afterlife."}]}

{"id": "28:81/q06", "question": "What events led to Qarun's destruction?", "turns_on": "The traditions give different immediate provocations: slander, a prayer contest, priestly rebellion, rejection of zakat, or general arrogance.", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q06/p1", "position": "After opposing Moses and resisting zakat, Qarun bribed a woman to accuse Moses falsely; she confessed and Moses appealed to God.", "reasons": "ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Ḥārith, Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī give the plot; al-Suddī calls her Shirta and says she received 2,000 dirhams; Ṭabrisī says 2,000 and marked money. {"id": "28:81/q16", "question": "What does فئة mean and how is it derived?", "turns_on": "The shared group sense is explained through differing roots: return, inclination or cutting.", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q16/p1", "position": "A group or band whose members support one another and can be called upon for help.", "reasons": "Majāz and Ṭabarī cite Khuffāf's poem for a strong, discerning group standing firm in hardship. Biqāʿī says those sharing his outlook perished while those fearing God would not petition for him, referring to 28:80."}, {"id": "28:81/q19/p3", "position": "His wealth, property and his own strength could supply no help.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr includes his wealth, servants and entourage; Jishumī connects this to the preceding warning against false patrons; Iṣlāḥī and Kuran Yolu make it an admonition against trusting wealth and power."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q20", "question": "What does من دون الله add to the denial of rescue?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q20/p1", "position": "No helper apart from or beyond God's aid could avert His decree.", "reasons": "Bursawī explicitly interprets the phrase as helpers beyond or apart from God's aid; Qatāda, Wāḥidī and Ṭabrisī say no army or faction could protect from God."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q21", "question": "What does المنتصرين mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the failed intisār is self-defense against punishment, retaliation against Moses, or victory with allies.", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q21/p1", "position": "People able to defend or save themselves against God's sinking.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Baghawī, Wāḥidī, Qurṭubī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Bayḍāwī, Bursawī, Biqāʿī, Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Ibn ʿĀshūr apply it to Qarun's inability to resist. Bayḍāwī, Nasafī and Bursawī explain naṣara/intāṣara as helping against an enemy and protecting oneself; Wāḥidī also defines al-muntaṣir as one attaining victory."}, {"id": "28:81/q21/p2", "position": "It can mean avenging himself on Moses.", "reasons": "Rāzī and Nasafī explicitly allow this alongside the sense of fending off divine punishment."}, {"id": "28:81/q21/p3", "position": "It can stress that Qarun gained no victory even with helpers.", "reasons": "Ālūsī presents this as an alternative emphasis; Ibn ʿĀshūr defines intasara as obtaining victory."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q22", "question": "What wider lesson does Qarun's ruin teach?", "turns_on": "The sources emphasize different lessons about riches, reliance, punishment and divine favor.", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q22/p1", "position": "Worldly wealth and power do not establish independent merit or safety; God's favor and final judgment decide the outcome.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says Qarun's knowledge-based claim to riches was exposed when wealth and strength failed, showing God granted them. Iṣlāḥī calls him a wealthy Jewish capitalist and says the wretched credit themselves and idols; his fate warns people seduced by riches who forget God and the Hereafter. Kuran Yolu says envious onlookers repented and recognized God's provision and the failure of ingratitude; Biqāʿī warns Muhammad's community against rejecting the mercy of his message, for prophets cannot force guidance or shield the condemned. Jishumī links it to false patrons and leaders giving no help."}, {"id": "28:81/q22/p2", "position": "The destruction is punishment for wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Jishumī labels the sinking punishment; Rāzī and Biqāʿī tie it to arrogance, disbelief and the reasoning that led Qarun astray."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q23", "question": "How does Qarun's fall connect to nearby verses?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of the surrounding passage supplies the link: the onlookers' reversal or the failure of false patrons.", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q23/p1", "position": "It reverses the crowd's wish in 28:79 and prepares their regret in 28:82.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī says the people who wanted Qarun's position regret it in the next verse. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the same onlookers witnessed the immediate punishment. Kuran Yolu says the formerly envious acknowledge God's provision and the failure of the ungrateful."}, {"id": "28:81/q23/p2", "position": "It demonstrates that following false patrons and leaders brings no protection.", "reasons": "Jishumī states this connection to the preceding lesson; Biqāʿī connects the failure of Qarun's party to God's allies in 28:80, who would not intercede for him."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q24", "question": "What does the account imply about divine لطف, the evil eye, and human acts?", "turns_on": "The theological applications address distinct consequences of the episode.", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q24/p1", "position": "God can destroy an admired person's worldly gift as لطف, teaching the person and admirers not to rely on it.", "reasons": "Jishumī applies this to Qarun's house and adornment: the deserving person learns favor is temporary and avoids conceit. He reports Abū Hāshim's use of the principle to affirm the evil eye, because the admirer likewise learns not to rely on worldly life."}, {"id": "28:81/q24/p2", "position": "The narrative offers indications that people originate their own acts.", "reasons": "Jishumī states this conclusion without further detail in the note."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q25", "question": "What other transmitted events illuminate swallowing or divine signs?", "turns_on": "The analogues are different narrated events and signs.", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q25/p1", "position": "Hadith describe a swaggering man swallowed by the earth and continuing to sink until Resurrection.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites al-Bukhārī's Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Hurayra versions, Aḥmad's Abū Saʿīd version about two green cloaks, whose chain he grades ḥasan and says Aḥmad alone transmits, and Abū Yaʿlā's Anas version about two cloaks."}, {"id": "28:81/q25/p2", "position": "A strange report tells of a proud young man in Najran who shrank and was carried off.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says Nawfal b. Musāḥiq reports a handsome, tall youth who claimed God marveled at him, then became a handspan high; a relative carried him away."}, {"id": "28:81/q25/p3", "position": "Biqāʿī compares other prophetic signs: a yearning trunk, Surāqa's sinking horse, and earth rejecting a defector's corpse.", "reasons": "At Ḥunayn the trunk yearned and chose Paradise over restoration. Surāqa's horse sank to its belly three times on the Hijra route; Muhammad spared him and foretold Kisra's bracelets, after which Surāqa embraced Islam. Anas reports a former scribe from Banū al-Najjār whose buried body was expelled twice after defecting to People of the Book; a second Christian-man version has three expulsions. Biqāʿī attributes them to Ṣaḥīḥ collections."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q26", "question": "How does the Torah account compare with the Qur'anic account?", "turns_on": "The comparison turns on the rebellion's motive, participants and event sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q26/p1", "position": "Numbers 16 supplies a fuller Korah rebellion narrative with priesthood dispute, earthquake and subsequent communal turmoil.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī quotes the tassel reminder from the fourth Torah book, then names Korah's lineage, Dathan, Abiram, On and 250 leaders. Dathan and Abiram accuse Moses of failed promises. Moses makes the earth-opening a test of his mission; households and property descend alive, 250 incense bearers die by fire, and Israel later blames Moses and Aaron. God then threatens the congregation, Aaron carries incense to stop a plague between living and dead, and 14,700 die besides those swallowed. The twelve staffs test the priesthood; Aaron's bears branches, leaves and almonds and is kept as a sign; later Aaron dies on Mount Hor and Eleazar succeeds him. Ibn ʿĀshūr summarizes Numbers 16; Iṣlāḥī says the Qur'an suppresses the mutual imprecation by the worship tent after Sāmirī."}, {"id": "28:81/q26/p2", "position": "The present Torah's account differs from the Ibn ʿAbbās plot narrative.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī specifically contrasts Numbers 16's named rebels and 250 leaders with the accusation story; he also notes the latter's focus on injury to Moses differs from the Qur'an's stated wrong to Israelites."}]}
{"id": "28:81/q27", "question": "What makes the wording of Qarun's destruction rhetorically striking?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:81/q27/p1", "position": "The story compresses ruin and admonition into exceptionally eloquent, well-ordered language.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī calls the three phrases harmonious and exceptional, saying Qur'anic stories combine narrative, admonition, wisdom, oneness and transcendence more coherently than expanded prose. He locates inimitability in wording, order, composition, clarity and eloquence, citing 3:138, 16:89, 26:195; he says placement and openings and endings move listeners to grief, joy, courage or generosity, and speaker identity shapes reception. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ quotes three words of the ruin as rarer than red sulfur and presents Bāqillānī's balanced order, sound, ease, vividness and demonstrative force. Jurjānī explains grandeur through implied attributes and cites Ziyād al-Aʿjam's poem locating generosity in a patron's dome rather than directly naming the man's traits."}]}
